timelineEvents.title: Move to Berlin
timelineEvents.label: c. 1926 · Move to Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue his musical education and professional development.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue music education.

timelineEvents.title: Private study and first Berlin networks
timelineEvents.label: 1926–1930 · Berlin study and networks
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper builds his Berlin career through private study with Moritz Mayer-Mahr and Walther Gmeindl, early publications, and collaboration with Fritz Rotter.
timelineEvents.longDescription: After moving to Berlin, Kaper developed his professional position through private study with pianist Moritz Mayer-Mahr and composer-conductor Walther Gmeindl, while also entering the German-language song market through Fritz Rotter and early publications under the title “Dr. Kaper.” By his own account in the 1975 oral-history interview, it was the composer Jerzy Fitelberg, among the friends he found in Berlin, who urged him to study privately rather than at the Hochschule. He had come to Berlin intending to enrol at the Staatliche Akademische Hochschule für Musik, but gave up the idea of a virtuoso career before the entrance examination, and a plan to study privately with Artur Schnabel foundered on the fees. Róża Etkin, whom he knew from the Chopin school in Warsaw, sent him to Mayer-Mahr, who urged him not to abandon the piano.

timelineEvents.title: Marriage
timelineEvents.label: 30 June 1927 · Marriage in Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora Sirot in Berlin.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora de domo Sirot in Berlin on June 30.

timelineEvents.title: Róża Etkin plays works by Kaper in Berlin
timelineEvents.label: Spring 1927 · Etkin plays Kaper in Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: In a Berlin recital reviewed in the spring of 1927, the Chopin prizewinner Róża Etkin played works by B. Kaper alongside Chopin and Szymanowski.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Signale für die musikalische Welt (no. 20, 1927) reported that Róża Etkin, a prizewinner at the first International Chopin Competition in Warsaw that January, gave a Berlin recital devoted partly to Chopin and partly to newer Polish composers, naming Szymanowski and B. Kaper. She played Chopin’s F minor Ballade, F-sharp minor Polonaise, four études, mazurkas and nocturnes; the notice does not name the works by Kaper.

timelineEvents.title: Jazz Piano Partnership
timelineEvents.label: 1928 · Jazz piano partnership
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper records jazz-influenced piano-duo arrangements with Hermann Biek, credited on the recordings as Hermann Bick, for Polydor.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Together with the pianist Hermann Biek, credited on records as Hermann Bick, Kaper recorded six two-piano arrangements for Deutsche Grammophon/Polydor in 1928: “The Varsity Drag”, “The Song Is Ended”, “Miss Annabelle Lee”, “Ice-Cream”, “My Inspiration” and “My Pet”. In the same year Das Theater listed Kaper at the Kabarett der Komiker performing “Jazz auf zwei Klavieren” in a duo with the pianist Sula Lewitsch.

timelineEvents.title: Earliest publications and recordings with Fritz Rotter
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Earliest Rotter publications
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The earliest published tangos and foxtrots by Kaper and Fritz Rotter documented here appear in German and Viennese editions.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Tangos and foxtrots by “Dr. Kaper” published in German and Viennese editions. Their working relationship is older than the printed songs: a manuscript of 1926 already places the two names together.

timelineEvents.title: Involvement in Polish cultural life in Berlin
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Polish cultural life in Berlin
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper remains active in Berlin’s Polish cultural life, including work with the Harmonia choir.
timelineEvents.longDescription: “Kurier Warszawski” reports on a concert by the Berlin choir “Harmonia”, directed by Kaper.

timelineEvents.title: Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
timelineEvents.label: 1929 · Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Bick und Kaper piano duo plays before a Berlin film premiere and attracts press attention.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung of 14 February 1929 reports that the evening at the Ufa-Theater Universum in Berlin, the première of Der Adjutant des Zaren with Ivan Mosjoukine and Carmen Boni, opened with the jazz piano duo Bick und Kaper, “die Jazz auf zwei Flügeln darboten”. The notice adds that their technique was astonishing.

timelineEvents.title: Earliest documented compositions for film
timelineEvents.label: 1930 · Earliest film compositions
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper’s earliest documented work for the cinema is music for three German sound films of 1930.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Music for Die lustigen Musikanten, directed by Max Obal, Alraune, directed by Richard Oswald, and Der Korvettenkapitän, directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein, all released in 1930. For Alraune Kaper wrote two tangos to words by Fritz Rotter, “Nur Tango, nur Tango” and “Wenn mich Männer betrügen”; Der Korvettenkapitän carried four of his songs, again to Rotter’s words.

timelineEvents.title: Meeting Walter Jurmann
timelineEvents.label: 1931 · Meeting Walter Jurmann
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Fritz Rotter pairs Kaper with Walter Jurmann in 1931, at the start of the partnership that shapes his European film career.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Fritz Rotter paired the two composers in 1931, when each had already had separate successes and sound film was multiplying commissions. Their names first stand together on Die große Attraktion, directed by Max Reichmann, but the printed credits for its songs are not uniform: “Du warst mir ein Roman”, the slow fox written for Richard Tauber, and “Das verliebte Orchester” were published with Kaper alone, while “Ich steh’ im Schnee und wart’ auf dich” and “Wir sind international” carry both names. The first film signed jointly throughout is Ehe mit beschränkter Haftung.

timelineEvents.title: Flourishing Berlin collaboration
timelineEvents.label: 1932 · Berlin collaboration flourishes
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper partnership flourishes across German films and popular songs.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Numerous German films with Jurmann–Kaper music, including “Hochzeitsreise zu dritt”, “Skandal in der Parkstraße”, “Es wird schon wieder besser”, “Der glückliche Herr Fünf”.

timelineEvents.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
timelineEvents.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
timelineEvents.longDescription: In 1933, after UFA terminated the contracts of its Jewish employees, Kaper and Jurmann left Berlin and, by way of Vienna, settled in Paris. His route ran through Vienna, where he had supervised the French version of Abenteuer am Lido, and the departure itself falls between the spring and the summer of 1933. Kaper’s oral history returns twice to an attack on him and his wife by a group of Nazis in a Berlin street, once within a story about self-defence and once as an aside to his account of film work, where he set it apart from his music. The attack does not explain his music, but it marks the point at which working conditions in the German film industry could no longer be separated from questions of safety.

timelineEvents.title: Songs beyond cinema
timelineEvents.label: 22 June 1934 · Songs beyond cinema
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs move beyond cinema into the French concert and festival repertoire.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs enter the French concert repertoire. At a summer festival in Montpellier, a jazz orchestra performs “Ninon, quand tu me souris” from “Tout pour l’amour” on an open-air stage.

timelineEvents.title: European afterlife
timelineEvents.label: 1934–1936 · European afterlife
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper films and songs continue circulating in Europe after the composers leave for America.
timelineEvents.longDescription: While the composers head to America, their European films and songs continue to circulate. In September 1934, “Madame wird kinderlieb” still plays in Stuttgart with Jurmann and Kaper credited — despite Nazi purges. In France, “Tout pour l’amour” with Kiepura screens as late as 1936; the Journal de Vichy calls their music “infiniment plaisante.” The inconsistency of the exclusion is visible earlier still: on 25 August 1933 the Westfälische Zeitung advertised Madame wird kinderlieb with the credit “Musik von Jurmann und Kaper” on the same page as an advertisement for a racist handbook of German ethnology.

timelineEvents.title: Earliest documented collaboration with Fritz Rotter
timelineEvents.label: First Rotter trace
timelineEvents.shortDescription: A 1926 manuscript of Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener documents an early collaboration between Kaper and Fritz Rotter, before sound film became his main professional platform.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The manuscript credit for Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener places Kaper beside Fritz Rotter at an early point in his Berlin years. It is an important transitional event: Rotter linked Kaper to the practical economy of the German hit song—publishers, performers, promotion, and sheet-music circulation—before those skills were absorbed into the machinery of early sound film. It also explains why Rotter later became the mediator who brought Kaper and Walter Jurmann together.

timelineEvents.title: Alraune as Kaper’s first documented sound-film commission
timelineEvents.label: Alraune and sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Alraune marks Kaper’s first clearly documented entry into early sound film, through songs rather than background scoring in the later Hollywood sense.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper’s first documented sound-film work belongs to the early phase of cinema in which the film composer’s task was still closely tied to song production. Alraune, Richard Oswald’s 1930 sound remake, did not yet require the later Hollywood model of continuous underscoring. Instead, Kaper contributed songs that could serve the film while also entering the wider economy of printed scores, records, performers, and radio.

timelineEvents.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
timelineEvents.label: Sängerfilm circuit
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.

timelineEvents.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
timelineEvents.label: Transnational sound film
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

timelineEvents.title: First performance of a work by Kaper at the Bach-Saal
timelineEvents.label: 3 December 1927 · First performance at the Bach-Saal
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Róża Etkin gives the first performance of a work by B. Kaper in her recital at the Bach-Saal in Berlin.
timelineEvents.longDescription: On 3 December 1927 Róża Etkin gave a recital at the Bach-Saal in Berlin whose programme — four Chopin ballades and works by Karol Szymanowski, Maurice Ravel and Isaac Albéniz, with Liszt’s Sonata in B minor — included the first performance of a work by B. Kaper. The announcement does not name the work. Kaper later recalled writing a piano sonatina for Etkin, which she played in Berlin; the Sonatina manuscript is dated 1927, but no source ties it to this recital rather than to her earlier one.

places.publicNote: Kaper’s principal German-period city, associated with his Berlin studies, cabaret and publishing networks, and early film work.
